Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Our goal is to ensure consistency between SciPy and NumPy in multivariate distribution broadcasting. The `size` parameter’s interaction with gufunc signatures is critical: it appears to control outer batch shape while leaving event dimensions (e.g., 3 in `(n)`) implicit. But we’re unsure whether this applies uniformly across `dirichlet`, `multivariate_hypergeometric`, or potential future distributions. Is this a deliberate design principle—or an informal convention we’re misinterpreting? We need clarity before committing to a pattern.

I accidentally discovered that nn.Linear with datatype float16/bfloat16 can produce significant numerical errors on sliced tensors:
 import torch
 torch.random.manual_seed(42)
 from torch import nn
 

 dtype = torch.float16
 batch, seq, embed_dim, delay = 2, 16, 4, 2
 x1 = torch.randn(batch, seq, embed_dim, device="cuda", dtype=dtype)
 x2 = x1[:, delay:]
 assert torch.allclose(x1[:, delay:], x2)
 net = nn.Linear(embed_dim, embed_dim).to("cuda").to(dtype=dtype)
 out1 = net(x1)
 out2 = net(x2)
 print((out1[:, delay:] - out2).abs().max())
 assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
 

 I got the output like this:
 tensor(0.0010, device='cuda:0', dtype=torch.float16, grad_fn=<MaxBackward1>)
 Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/jewel/Workspaces/cusrl/test.py", line 14, in <module>
  assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
 AssertionError
 

 If the type is bfloat16, the error is even greater:
 tensor(0.0078, device='cuda:0', dtype=torch.bfloat16, grad_fn=<MaxBackward1>)
 Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/jewel/Workspaces/cusrl/test.py", line 14, in <module>
  assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
 AssertionError
 

 However, if the tensor is cloned after sliced x2 = x1[:, delay:].clone() or the type is float32, it will produce an error of exactly zero.
 tensor(0., device='cuda:0', grad_fn=<MaxBackward1>)
 

 I don't know if this is an allowable margin of error or a bug.
rephrased_statement: Why does nn.Linear exhibit numerical divergence on sliced float16 tensors? The code `x2 = x1[:, 2:]` yields mathematically equivalent data to `x1[:, 2:]`, yet `net(x2)` and `net(x1)[:, 2:]` differ by up to 0.001–0.008 in FP16/BF16. The discrepancy disappears with `.clone()` or higher precision. Is this behavior documented? Should we be cloning every sliced input to linear layers in mixed-precision training?

 import timeit

 with torch.no_grad():

  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

>>> a.mean = lambda : 0

  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: We’re implementing consistent broadcasting semantics across SciPy’s multivariate distributions and are modeling behavior after NumPy’s `multinomial` PR, where `size=(10, 4, 2)` on inputs with shapes `n: (4,1)` and `pvals: (2,3)` yields output shape `(10,4,2,3)`. The key insight is that `size` controls the batch dimensions, not the full output shape—the last dimension comes from the distribution’s intrinsic support. But we’re uncertain whether this pattern was consciously adopted across all distributions, or if it’s an emergent artifact. Do we have explicit guidance on how `size` must behave with non-scalar parameters like `cov` or `alpha`?

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken

    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)

TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: In NumPy, when `size=(10, 4, 2)` is passed to `multinomial`, the output has shape `(10, 4, 2, 3)`—the last dimension comes from the gufunc output signature `(n)`. But for `multivariate_normal`, whose signature is `(n),(n,n) -> (n)`, does `size` operate identically? We don’t know whether this is a documented feature or an accidental consistency. We need to know: is it a requirement that `size` only affects the batch dimensions, and never the output dimensionality derived from parameter shapes?

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)
rephrased_statement: I thought NumPy’s interoperability meant 'if it looks array-like, convert it' — turns out it’s 'if it has a .mean method, call it with NumPy’s signature'. I set a .mean = None on an object to disable some logic, and np.mean() crashed because it tried to invoke None(). Then I set a lambda, and it crashed again because no axis= argument. I had zero idea this was how NumPy worked. Is this behavior stable? Should I avoid any .mean attributes on my classes?

Because, we do take an existing well defined URI of scheme file and turn that into vscode-userdata. Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s

 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: We're trying to unify broadcasting behavior across SciPy's multivariate distributions, but I'm uncertain: should size=(...) behave identically in multivariate_normal(mean, cov, size=(10,)) as it does in multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10,))? The gufunc signatures suggest consistency is possible, but I don't know if NumPy intends for size to exclude the last dimension universally.

Thank you so much for the detailed and insightful analysis.

I followed your suggestion and tested with:

torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False

As you anticipated, export on GPU succeeded when disabling cuDNN. This strongly indicates that the issue is indeed related to certain cuDNN-optimized fused kernels, likely being incorrectly traced during export when fake tensors are used.

For completeness, my environment reports the following cuDNN version:

torch.backends.cudnn.version() == 90100

This further supports the hypothesis that some low-level dispatch or fusion within cuDNN is not being properly marked as opaque or guarded during export tracing?

self.rnn = nn.RNN(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True)

This confirms that the problem is not limited to LSTM, but more broadly affects cuDNN-backed recurrent layers, including nn.RNN. Disabling torch.backends.cudnn.enabled continues to serve as a valid workaround in both cases.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: We’ve noticed that `multinomial`’s broadcasting model treats `size` as a batch controller independent of event shape, and we’d like to replicate that in SciPy. But we’re uncertain whether this model extends naturally to distributions with more complex parameter structures, such as `multivariate_normal` where the covariance matrix is 2D. Should `size=(2,3)` applied to `mean=(5,)` and `cov=(5,5)` produce shape `(2,3,5)`? We don’t know if NumPy has a consistent rule here—or if different distributions were designed with different expectations.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: As we add broadcasting support to SciPy’s multivariate distributions, we’re trying to map the semantics of `size` consistently with NumPy’s existing patterns. For instance, in `rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10,4,2))`, the output shape is `(10,4,2,3)`—the last dimension comes from the gufunc signature `(n) -> (n)`, while `(10,4,2)` is the broadcast shape of inputs. But for `multivariate_normal(mean, cov, size=...)`, does `size` behave the same? We don’t know if NumPy treats all gufunc-like signatures uniformly, and we want to avoid introducing divergent semantics. Is this documented behavior, or are we guessing?

Because, we do take an existing well defined URI of scheme file and turn that into vscode-userdata. Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)

>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: I'm seeing a 2x performance regression when running BERT inference on MPS compared to CPU, even though the MPS backend is active (98% GPU utilization, 15W power spike). The same code on CUDA achieves ~44x faster speeds. Is this expected given the current state of MPS optimization for transformer models, or is there a known bottleneck with embedding layers or attention kernel dispatch on Apple Silicon?

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):

  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)
rephrased_statement: I thought numpy’s interoperability meant it’d safely convert objects to arrays — turns out it prefers calling .mean() if present, even if it’s broken for numpy’s expectations. A polars Series with .mean() breaks np.mean() because it doesn’t accept 'axis'. This is terrifying. How many other libraries are silently incompatible with this hidden contract?

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)

Thinking a bit more about this, I wonder if URI should statically allow us to register a scheme to behave like a file scheme. Because, we do take an existing well defined URI of scheme file and turn that into vscode-userdata. This in turn means, every client that deals with such a URI would need to ensure that the scheme is converted back to file before using the URI. That seems fragile.

If we could tell URI to treat vscode-userdata like a file scheme, maybe the change would be easier and less fragile?
rephrased_statement: It’s surprising that URI doesn’t provide a way to declare that a custom scheme (like vscode-userdata) should be treated as equivalent to file:. We’re effectively re-implementing file semantics in every consumer. This feels like a missing abstraction — why not let the system know that this scheme = file, and handle it transparently?

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: I’m trying to understand if the ~2x slowdown of BERT on MPS compared to CPU is a systemic limitation. The GPU is clearly active (98% utilization, 15W+ power), and the code matches Hugging Face’s recommended setup. Given CUDA achieves 40x speedup, is MPS simply not optimized for attention-heavy models yet? Or is there an unrecognized bottleneck I’m missing?

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: We want consistency between SciPy and NumPy multivariate distributions, but I'm unclear on whether the size parameter's interaction with broadcasting is formally specified. For example, should multivariate_normal(mean, cov, size=(3,4)) always return shape (3,4,n), regardless of mean/cov shapes? I don't know if this is guaranteed or just current behavior.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)

TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)

>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)

Because, we do take an existing well defined URI of scheme file and turn that into vscode-userdata. This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: In NumPy’s multivariate distributions, `size` affects output shape alongside parameter broadcasting, but it doesn’t include the event dimension. For example, `multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))` produces `(10, 4, 2, 3)`. Is this behavior intentional and consistent across `multivariate_normal`, `dirichlet`, etc.? We want to avoid introducing inconsistencies in SciPy’s implementations.

Thank you so much for the detailed and insightful analysis.

I followed your suggestion and tested with:

torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False

As you anticipated, export on GPU succeeded when disabling cuDNN. This strongly indicates that the issue is indeed related to certain cuDNN-optimized fused kernels, likely being incorrectly traced during export when fake tensors are used.

torch.backends.cudnn.version() == 90100

This further supports the hypothesis that some low-level dispatch or fusion within cuDNN is not being properly marked as opaque or guarded during export tracing?

self.rnn = nn.RNN(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True)

This confirms that the problem is not limited to LSTM, but more broadly affects cuDNN-backed recurrent layers, including nn.RNN. Disabling torch.backends.cudnn.enabled continues to serve as a valid workaround in both cases.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: In designing uniform parameter handling across multivariate distributions, we’re evaluating whether the `size` parameter should always prepend batch dimensions without touching the core variate dimension implied by the gufunc signature (e.g., `(n)` for `dirichlet`, `(n,n)` for `cov` in `multivariate_normal`). We see this in `multinomial`’s new behavior, but we’re not sure if this is an officially sanctioned design or an emergent implementation quirk. Without documented semantics, we risk introducing inconsistency—what if `multivariate_normal` is expected to treat `size` as the full output shape, not just the outer batch? We need to know the intended contract.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: The MPS backend is clearly being utilized during BERT inference — GPU power spikes, Activity Monitor shows heavy load — yet performance is worse than CPU. I expected near-CUDA-level gains given the hardware, but instead I’m seeing a 2x slowdown. Is this a known limitation of the current MPS stack with transformer models? Or is there a hidden bottleneck in how PyTorch handles sequence padding, embedding lookups, or multi-head attention on Metal? I'm not sure what aspects of the model architecture are causing this underutilization.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: In NumPy, `rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=s)` produces an output with shape `s + (n,)`, where `s` is the broadcast shape of inputs and `(n,)` comes from the gufunc signature. But for `multivariate_normal(mean, cov, size=s)`, the output is `s + (mean.shape[-1],)`. I’m unsure whether this consistency is guaranteed or coincidental—should SciPy enforce this pattern, or is it an implementation detail we shouldn’t rely on?

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: We're trying to unify SciPy’s multivariate distribution interfaces with NumPy’s. Key uncertainty: when `size=(a, b)` is passed with broadcastable parameters, is the output always `[a, b] + event_shape`? For example, with `multivariate_normal(mean, cov, size=(2, 3))` where mean.shape=(4,) → output shape `(2, 3, 4)`. Is this guaranteed, or are we risking future incompatibility?

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)

TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean

           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: We're trying to standardize the interface for multivariate distribution sampling in SciPy, particularly how `size` integrates with parameter broadcasting. Based on `multinomial`'s behavior in the PR, `size` controls the outer batch dimensions while leaving the output's last dimension (e.g., `n` in `(n)`) untouched. But we don’t know if this design was intentional for all distributions, or if `multivariate_normal` with `(n),(n,n)->(n)` should treat `size` differently when `mean` or `cov` are higher-rank arrays. Is this a de facto standard, or an accidental implementation detail?

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: I can't figure out why MPS is slower than CPU for BERT inference. The code is identical to my CUDA setup, which is blazing fast. I've ruled out misconfiguration—device is set, tensors are on MPS, no gradients. Is this a known issue with layer normalization or attention kernels in MPS? Or should I just avoid it for now?

Thinking a bit more about this, I wonder if URI should statically allow us to register a scheme to behave like a file scheme. Because, we do take an existing well defined URI of scheme file and turn that into vscode-userdata. This in turn means, every client that deals with such a URI would need to ensure that the scheme is converted back to file before using the URI. That seems fragile.

If we could tell URI to treat vscode-userdata like a file scheme, maybe the change would be easier and less fragile?
rephrased_statement: It feels fragile that every client needs to know to transform vscode-userdata:// URIs back to file:// before accessing resources. Why not allow registering vscode-userdata as a scheme that behaves identically to file: internally? That way, the URI library handles the mapping, and consumers don’t have to worry about it — less boilerplate, fewer bugs.

Thinking a bit more about this, I wonder if URI should statically allow us to register a scheme to behave like a file scheme. Because, we do take an existing well defined URI of scheme file and turn that into vscode-userdata. This in turn means, every client that deals with such a URI would need to ensure that the scheme is converted back to file before using the URI. That seems fragile.

If we could tell URI to treat vscode-userdata like a file scheme, maybe the change would be easier and less fragile?
rephrased_statement: It seems fragile that clients must manually rewrite `vscode-userdata://` URIs back to `file://` before any filesystem operation. Given that this mapping is application-level and deterministic, could the URI class offer a built-in mechanism to declare scheme aliases? For instance, registering `vscode-userdata` as a pseudo-file scheme would let us delegate path resolution semantics to the underlying file system without requiring every consumer to implement the same translation logic.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: We’re adding broadcasting support to SciPy’s multivariate distributions and need to know: does NumPy’s `size` parameter always describe the batch shape *excluding* the event dimension (like `(n)` in gufunc signatures)? For instance, in `multivariate_normal(mean, cov, size=(5, 3))`, is the output shape `(5, 3, d)` by design? We’re unsure if this is a contract we can rely on.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: For consistency across SciPy and NumPy, we need to know: When `size` is passed to a multivariate distribution, should it describe the batch shape only — excluding the output variate dimension implied by the distribution’s signature — or should it define the entire output shape? I’m not sure whether this distinction is formally specified anywhere, or if it’s just inferred from `multinomial`’s behavior.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: We’re adapting SciPy’s multivariate distributions to support broadcasting similar to NumPy’s `multinomial`, but we’re uncertain about the semantics of the `size` parameter. Specifically, does `size=(10, 4, 2)` mean 'generate 10 samples for each of 4×2 parameter combinations', leaving the variate dimension (e.g., 3 for multinomial) to be appended automatically? Or does it intend to fully specify the final output shape? We have no documentation confirming this, and we’re unsure whether this behavior is intentional across distributions or an implementation artifact we should avoid replicating.

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)
rephrased_statement: I just broke my code by adding a .mean attribute to a class, and np.mean started throwing 'NoneType is not callable'. Now I realize NumPy is doing duck-typing so aggressively it ignores semantics. Is this intentional? Or is this a bug no one noticed because it’s too weird?
